claim: Forecast error is mostly grid-cell height: a 6.5 K/km fix cut IFS error from 2.8 K to 1.7 K.
data_label: open data: MeteoSwiss stations + Open-Meteo forecasts, Aug-Oct 2026
limit: Only 92 days, one autumn, ten stations; no winter and no confidence intervals yet.
alt: Line chart of 2 m temperature error against forecast lead time for two models, raw and height-corrected. The corrected lines sit well below the raw ones.
post:
Your phone says 12 degrees. The station on the hill says 7. Who is wrong?

I wanted to know how far a point forecast drifts from what a Swiss weather station actually measured, so I built a small open-source tool that pairs hourly forecasts with station observations and scores bias, MAE and RMSE per station, lead time and variable.

I ran it over August to October 2026 at ten stations, from 273 m to 3571 m, 703,791 forecast/observation pairs. One day ahead, the 2 km ICON-CH2 model was off by 1.7 K on average for 2 m temperature. The 25 km ECMWF IFS was off by 2.8 K, mostly because its grid cell sits at the wrong height. Shifting the forecast from grid height to station height with a plain 6.5 K/km lapse rate brought IFS down to 1.7 K.

What is not verified: this is one autumn, so no winter inversions or snow, there are no confidence intervals, and Open-Meteo's previous-runs archive is a derived product, not raw model output. The correction over-shoots on summits like Jungfraujoch.

If you compare forecasts to ground truth, which error would you want to see first: bias, MAE, or something event-based?

Code: https://github.com/Usernamepersonperson/forecast-vs-station-drift
